pitch_detail.notes: A brief approach pitch that passes a chockstone. The belay is on the left at a fixed pin, roughly 20 ft before the ice starts.
Steep ice up a chimney, then a step left onto a hanging curtain, which is the ice crux. Sling the large chockstone where the ice finishes to belay.
Cross left over big blocks with poor footholds, then go directly up through a V-shaped roof slot, the mixed crux. Belay just above on a pin, or push on to a better ledge where gear is minimal.
Head left up the ramp; the difficulty is anywhere from 5.5 to 5.8 depending on the line you take.

review.changed: Wrote P1-P3 and a combined P4-5 entry. Lengths converted from feet for P1 and P2. Cruxes on P2 (ice) and P3 (mixed), both named. No rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.6 does not describe a route whose cruxes are ice and mixed climbing.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin in the loose 5.6 chimney of the neighbouring route and break left onto the face about two-thirds of the way up, wherever the features allow. Slightly runout 5.7 face climbing leads to a ledge, where you set an anchor under the double crack system left of the long roof. Pitch lengths are approximate.

Easy ground leads to a small alcove or roof at the foot of the double cracks, then the climbing steadily steepens to a well-protected crux. Place the #4, make overhanging moves out of the crack and mantel left onto a small ledge. Belay options are poor; small hand-size pieces make a workable anchor.

Traverse left into the obvious squeeze chimney. After leaving it, climb a bit higher and follow the best protection right toward a curving right-facing corner, which gives slabby 5.7 climbing. At its top break left on the easiest line to a good belay near the top of the wall.
Low fifth-class ground to the ridge crest, with a belay in a crack just beneath the summit and the start of the walk-off.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with stated grades; lengths converted from feet and flagged as approximate. Crux on P2. No rappels.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.10b/c; the crux pitch is described as 5.10c.

pitch_detail.notes: The slab pitch. Mossy cracks up the low-angle slab are cleaner than they look; an option begins higher on the left and traverses in. Once on the mossy ledge above the cracks, clip a bolt overhead and move left to a stance, where the slab gets steeper. Climb the very thin slab straight to the second bolt, which is hard to clip, then good flakes trending right. A small cam fits above the second bolt. Carry on up and to the right until you reach the base of the dihedral and keep a #2 and #3 Camalot for the belay. A confident slab climber should lead it.

The flake pitch. Traverse left past a couple of chockstones to an awkward move around the point into the dihedral, then a long sustained stretch of liebacking and stemming on knobs. Belay on a small ledge at the top of the dihedral with stoppers and finger-size cams.

A very short finger crack and some knobby face reach a little ledge under a dihedral that faces right; lieback that dihedral up a series of ledges. Cams from 0.75 to 3 fit. Belay on the middle ledges and treat the short upper stretch as its own pitch so the leader can be watched at the bolt.

Go directly up across ledges to a shallow 0.75 placement below the bolt. Reach the jug, clip, and pull one bouldery move to the ledge above. The original line zig-zagged far left then back right to the same ledge.

The best pitch on the route: an exposed dihedral and ramp take you to its end, where you move right onto a jug and mantel (a #1 or #2 Camalot helps). Another step right and a short dihedral lead to a ledge close to the top. Large stoppers are useful, and a few spare slings help with the final traverse.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches with stated grades; lengths converted from approximate feet only where stated (~180, ~150, ~110 ft). Bolts only where counted from the description. Crux not set. No rappels.
review.other_findings: Stored 5 pitches and 5.10+ agree; the description calls it four or five pitches.

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble blocky ground, trending left to the foot of a chockstone chimney.
Climb the chimney, passing a big jammed block, then easier moves reach a ledge. Belay to the right of the tombstone.
A V-slot that opens out into much easier terrain. Belay under a double-cornered ramp.
Take either the right or left corner; good turf for axes the whole way. The pitch ends right of and below a chockstone chimney, where a solid anchor can be made with two axes.

A smooth chimney with more steepness than it appears, rising to the final chockstone roof, which is the crux. The reachy move is well covered by a 0.75 placed to the right of the block. Then a short run to a scenic ledge belay.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches; lengths converted from feet. Crux P5. No rappels: exit left and downclimb.
review.other_findings: Stored M4+ vs. the highest stated grade M4.

pitch_detail.notes: Many splitter cracks start the route. The standout is a 5.9 crack on the left that runs from hand to fist size, and further left is a 5.6 corner system of good rock. A good belay ledge comes after about 30 m.
Around 5.5, blocky and ledgy, best broken into 30 m pitches.
The tombstone pitch: a 0.75 to 2 inch crack splitting a roughly 25 m panel, to a big ledge above. The grade is unclear: 5.7 or possibly 5.10a. An easier way sneaks up the left side.
Lead on to the Hero Traverse, where you can either bail off to the right or keep climbing.
Free-choice cracks on lower-angle rock and short steps with a hard move or two, leading to the top of the Sunshine Wall.
A low-angle splitter that protects better than it appears, with good face holds and hidden jams, and a lovely view of the chasm on the left. A fine finish.

review.changed: Wrote 6 entries covering P1-P8 (P2-3 and P6-7 each combined as the description does). Tombstone pitch grade is uncertain so left out of the grade field.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.10a only matches the uncertain tombstone grade; other pitches are 5.9 or easier.

pitch_detail.notes: The notes here cover the right-hand (north) start: a distinct corner facing right, holding a wide crack, at around 12,500 ft, with a small horn emerging from the tundra at its foot. Climb the wide corner crack for 50 ft, using smaller cracks for gear to avoid the offwidth. Above, vague dihedrals and slab, a bit bushy; gear may need excavating with a nut tool. Belay at small trees.

Roughly 600 ft of rope but only about 400 ft of height gained, 5.6 to 5.8. Continue up vague dihedrals to a tree ledge, then go left and up, staying on the ridge or just left of it; expect brief boulder problems offering choices, with runouts that are manageable, as the ridge steepens. Move right along a grassy ledge for something like 40 ft to reach a clean, left-slanting crack about 50 ft tall that goes from hands to wide hands. If you step right too early, you can still see the crack and cross to it.
Quality improves here: hands to fists up to an airy perch, then a few steps with short cruxes to a notch and a chasm. The chasm is not that deep but feels exposed.

Cross the chasm into a groove; gear is abundant for the crossing and higher. Struggle up the groove, a bit of easy grass, then a hand-and-finger crack or layback. A last bulge is less hard than it looks. Belay here or continue 30 ft of easy ledge.
Three cracks split the short final headwall; 5.7 to 5.9 depending on the choice. The left one may be easiest, the middle has one short hard layback move to jams, and the right is unknown.

review.changed: Wrote P1, a combined P2-4 entry, and P5-P7, with stated grades and feet converted to metres. P2-4 range and P7 range kept in notes. No crux set. No rappels: the way out climbs up and right.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.9+ PG13 vs. the highest stated grade 5.9.

pitch_detail.notes: Bolted slab, lumpy and easy-angled, ending at a wide ledge with anchors toward the climber's right.
Begin on the bolt line 10 ft left of the anchor and finish on a large ledge under a roof. Linking this with the next pitch gives a long pitch of the route's best climbing.
Take the arete to the right of the belay. A harder move, then a leftward traverse above the lip of the overhang, forms the crux. Mantel into the broad dihedral and end on a large ledge.
Pull a small overhang off the ledge, move up and right, up a small wedge, then bolts onto the left arete. Ends on a large ledge with an anchor.
Straight up the bolted slab to the anchor at the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches with stated grades; lengths converted from feet. Crux on P3. No rappel table: only 'rap the route with a 70 m rope' is stated.
review.other_findings: None.

pitch_detail.notes: Bolted slab climbing to a two-bolt anchor on a wide ledge. With a 70 m rope and careful rope handling it can be linked onward.

Climb the pillar to the right of a bolted dihedral that runs into the evident chimney. Off the anchor, a gentle step gets you to the pillar's base; reach a ledge, use the little dihedral to the left, then cross right on face holds above a small roof to a solid stance. That sequence is the hardest part and is more difficult for shorter climbers. Next comes a brief fist-and-hand crack, a second roof, and a roomy ledge holding a two-bolt anchor.
A short pitch of ideal hand cracks to a small roof, over it to a two-bolt anchor on the big grassy Lunch Break Ledge.
Move the belay into an alcove below the roof, where gear is good. Get over the roof with a #5, then moderate terrain leads directly to two bolts.
Either broken 5.6 ground or an unidentified sport pitch to the left; both finish at chains on top of the formation.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches. Crux P4 (top grade). No rappel table: stations not listed in order, only 'rappel the route with a 70 m' or a single rappel off the north face.
review.other_findings: None.

pitch_detail.notes: Easy-ish but runout climbing on small gear, angling up and left along a broken line of cracks to reach a belay ledge.
Moderate ground on small gear to the foot of a steep hand crack. A bouldery move gets into the crack, then it is a sprint to the belay ledge.

Step high onto the face to the left of the belay, then delicate moves reach a steep corner. Stem up it to a protection bolt, swing out left through the roof with a lot of air beneath you, clip a second bolt, then moderate climbing reaches the anchor.

This is the Fridge Handle finish: a scruffy, blocky chimney to the left of the belay, topping out on the Anvil. Treat the handle it is named for with care if you pull on it. A direct variation up a dirty chimney right above the belay is also 5.6.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches. No lengths stated. No crux set (two 5.11 pitches). Variation noted in P4.
review.other_findings: None.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on the sloping ledge: a shallow, blocky dihedral just right of the north arete. Above, low fifth-class ground follows the ridge crest to a comfortable platform. The pitch can be skipped by going up the main gully between this peak and the neighbouring one to a ramp back to the ridge.
Take the ramp to the left below the sharp arete, reach the Crow's Nest, then mantel or turn the exposed corner (with a piton) to the north summit. Protects easily on a range of cams.
Move along the overhanging, airy knife edge to the real (south) summit. Long slings and cams up to #1 are adequate; a slip toward the east side would be serious.

rappel_detail.notes: Starts from the south summit and drops about 90 ft into a grassy gully facing northwest. An 80 m rope may reach the bottom.
Traverse on rappel left around a shallow corner and thread the dirty pinch; about 40 to 50 ft down into the south gully between this peak and the neighbouring one.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches and a 2-rappel table. Anchor of rappel 2 is hedged and its length is a range, so only in notes. Historical narrative omitted.
review.other_findings: Stored descent text 'reverse the route, or rappel' agrees.

pitch_detail.notes: Access pitch to a good belay ledge just under the main difficulties. Traverse around the corner past a neighbouring route, then look up for grassy ledges to the foot of the wide crack. A bolted anchor three-quarters up belongs to a different route and could serve; a better ledge is about 20 ft higher. You can rappel from the top to that ledge and skip this pitch.

Begin up a thin left-facing dihedral system until the crack ends at a good hand jam. Shift 5 ft to the right into the wide crack and stem and jam upward until a steep hand crack opens in the right-hand wall; this takes you to the closing squeeze chimney and the belay ledge.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches; lengths converted from feet. Crux P2 (top grade). No rappel table.
review.other_findings: None.

pitch_detail.notes: Start with a couple of meandering slab boulders that give onto a crack system leaning right. Once the rock turns orange, fractured and loose, veer right toward a bush. The anchors are on the left face, left of and below the bush. Mellow climbing with decent gear.

Two cruxes: the first immediately right of the anchors with little protection. You can clip the first-pitch anchors and build another just above the bush. Go past the bush, left over the bulge, then right on thin footholds with poor gear.
A ramp of bulges and slab to the next anchor; fun, runout climbing.
Go left of the anchors and clip a face-height bolt on the nearest shelf. Then run it out up and left before the first pieces. Continue to a grassy ledge. Can link with the next pitch.

Straight up from the anchors, veer left onto a ramp and take it back right toward the anchors by the trees on the ledge, where a walkable area has anchors behind a tree. An alternate finish goes right of the anchors to the top anchors of a neighbouring route, about 40 ft away.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches. Crux P2 (top grade, two cruxes named). No rappel table: only the first of four rappels is described.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.8 agrees.

pitch_detail.notes: An easy ramp to a small tree.
Steep wall past a few gear placements and a bolt, then more steep ground with good gear, the crux, to a ledge under a fist and offwidth crack. Anchor there. The pitch could be split in two.
Fist and offwidth crack past a bolt, then the easiest line up and right to the top. Could also be split in two.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches; P2 and P3 have no stated grade. Crux P2. No rappel table: the descent is on a neighbouring route.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.9+ is not stated per pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: A superb hand crack runs up the left of a massive dihedral. Where it narrows to a seam, move a few feet left, then good holds lead up and back to the right to a foot ledge and a gear anchor.
Traverse left from the anchor to a bolt, then follow a highly exposed arete to a big ledge with one bolt and a thin crack beside it. Build a gear anchor.
Up and left toward a right-facing flake, stand on it and follow the crack system in good rock above; this is the crux. Belay on the next ledge with gear.
Good holds on good rock to another fine belay ledge. Build the anchor just under the ledge.
Into a left-facing dihedral, then the easiest line to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches with lengths converted from feet; no pitch grades stated. Crux P3. No rappel table: the descent uses a neighbouring route.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.9- PG13 not stated per pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: Fun face climbing up a weakness to a ledge with a bolted anchor.
A step or two left of the anchor, follow the weakness up to the crux, then an exciting traverse right onto exposed face, good holds and easier ground to another ledge with a bolted anchor.

From the anchor, climb past a big flake shaped like a tooth to a small ledge. Take the cracks just left of a short corner, then step right onto a large flake that leads up to a ledge with a bolted anchor.
The easiest line to the top, then step right to a bolted anchor.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with lengths converted from feet. Crux P2. No rappel table: four rappels along the bolted anchors with a single 60 m rope are mentioned but not listed as stations.
review.other_findings: None.

pitch_detail.notes: The route starts at a bolted ski-mountaineering anchor. Bolts and a few gear placements mark the line; one 2 inch cam and a 0.75 cam or brown tricam cover the gear. The upper section is cruxy.

Two bolts lead to a huge flake system; follow it beyond a bolted anchor up to the next ledge, where a tree serves as a natural belay. This is the route's crux, and the pitch could be divided into two.
Traverse a ledge system 120 ft right to a bolted anchor, gaining about 50 ft of height.
Move right onto the arete and follow it across solid, blocky low fifth-class terrain; return left at the end to a bolted anchor.
Go right around a rib, then the cracks on the exposed arete carry you to the summit. Probably the best pitch of the route.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches with lengths converted from feet. Crux P2. No rappel table: the rappel route is described in outline (five 30 m rappels) not station by station.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.8 PG13 consistent.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb all the WI2 slab, 50 to 60 m, to a sheltered belay behind the pillar. Reaching the top in a single 60 m pitch needs climbing well over halfway up the slab, so two pitches are suggested.
The short pillar, then easier, thinner ice, 30 to 40 m, topping out near a small tree on the left.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches; both lengths are stated as ranges, so they stay in the notes and lengthM is omitted. No rappel table: one long rappel off a tree is described.
review.other_findings: Stored WI5 reflects the pillar; P1 is WI2. The route sits in an avalanche funnel.

pitch_detail.notes: Clean face split by good cracks, ending at a ledge for the belay.
Traverse a ledge system from east to west on easy ground.
Scramble up to the base of the next pitch.
One or two bouldery, unprotected moves into a small corner where gear appears; this is the crux. Then step up and right and take the easiest path through steep ground to a big ledge.
Easy ground trending up and left leads to the bottom of a huge, gently angled corner that faces left.
Cracks in the middle of the ramp left of the corner itself. Belay about three-quarters of the way up.
Climb to the top of the ramp or corner, then traverse up and around to the north side and follow the easiest path to a good belay ledge just under the summit.
A short scramble to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 8 pitches (stored count is 5); lengths converted from feet. Crux P4. No rappels: walk-off.
review.other_findings: Stored 5 pitches vs. 8 described; the stated pitch lengths sum to roughly 220 m against stored 198 m.

pitch_detail.notes: A ramp to a ledge.
Continue up the ramp almost to its end, then make a crusty traverse left into a big corner system.
Climb the corner system, with an overhanging splitter hand crack leading to easier ground. Belay there.
Easy ground heading up and left, to a ledge close under the summit.
An easy scramble to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches; lengths converted from feet. Crux not set (not stated). No rappels.
review.other_findings: Stored 4 pitches; description has 4 roped plus a short summit scramble.

pitch_detail.notes: Follow a hand-and-fist crack beyond a small ledge to a larger one and anchor there.
Climb the 5.6 ground above the belay, which is the crux, to a belay ledge. An easier variation goes up a weakness to the right.
Traverse the ledge east for 100 ft, so you move your belay along it.
A weakness leads to a large ledge near the summit, with exposed and pleasant climbing; the pitch can be divided into several.
An easy scramble to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 5 entries; lengths converted from feet. Crux P2 named. No rappels.
review.other_findings: Stored 4 pitches; description has 4 roped plus a short summit scramble.
